title: Document-Level Event Factuality Identification via Reinforced Semantic Learning Network
research_question: Can document-level event factuality be identified end to end by jointly encoding event and document semantics while learning to select the sentences and tokens most relevant to the target event?
methodology: The paper formulates document-level event factuality identification as assigning a document-wide factuality value to a target event even when sentences mentioning or discussing it carry differing local factuality. RSLN uses multi-granularity hierarchical semantic encoding together with hierarchical reinforcement learning to select event-relevant sentences and tokens while filtering irrelevant or noisy text. Its encoders combine event information, intra-sentence semantics, and document-topic information before producing the document-level prediction. The model is evaluated on the newly annotated English and Chinese ExDLEF corpus and compared with multiple neural baselines, with additional component ablations and text-selection analyses.

key_findings.finding: The paper explicitly observes that sentence-level factualities concerning an event may differ within a document while defining the document-level factuality as a single value.
On ExDLEF, RSLN reports macro/micro F1 of 67.42/77.48 for English and 75.74/78.29 for Chinese, outperforming the reported comparison systems.
Ablation results identify the event encoder and topic-context encoder as two of the most important components: removing them produces substantial macro- and micro-F1 losses in both languages.

Sentence selection has a larger measured effect than token selection: removing SPNet reduces macro-F1 by 4.07 points in English and 4.64 in Chinese, compared with 1.35 and 0.85 points when TPNet is removed.
ExDLEF contains 5,030 English instances and 5,150 Chinese instances across Uu, CT-, PS-, PS+, and CT+ factuality categories.
The paper identifies insufficient direct evaluation of selected-sentence quality and limited deep interpretability of the model as an experimental limitation.

limitations: The model assigns one document-level factuality value, so differing local mentions are collapsed rather than preserved as an explicit temporal revision trajectory.
The authors identify inadequate direct evaluation of selected sentences and limited deep interpretability as limitations.
Multi-event document-level factuality and cross-document factuality are left for future work.
ExDLEF is highly imbalanced; for example, the English portion contains 3,532 CT+ instances but only 42 Uu and 51 PS- instances.
The main reported per-class F1 comparisons emphasize CT-, PS+, and CT+, giving much less empirical evidence about the rare factuality categories.
The formulation does not explicitly encode workflow transitions such as planned-to-confirmed, planned-to-canceled, completed-to-corrected, or superseded-by-later-message.
Performance on workplace email and dialogue is not evaluated.
raw_claims: Document-level event factuality is defined from the perspective of the whole document.
Sentence-level factuality values for the same target event may differ within a document.
RSLN selects relevant sentences and tokens using hierarchical reinforcement learning.
The representation combines event, sentence-level, and document-level semantic information.
ExDLEF contains both English and Chinese sub-corpora.
The English ExDLEF portion contains 5,030 instances and the Chinese portion contains 5,150.
RSLN reaches macro-F1 67.42 and micro-F1 77.48 on the English ExDLEF evaluation.
RSLN reaches macro-F1 75.74 and micro-F1 78.29 on the Chinese ExDLEF evaluation.
Event and topic-context encoders make large contributions in the ablation study.
Sentence selection has a larger ablation effect than token selection.
The paper does not precisely evaluate the performance of its selected sentences or provide deep model interpretability.
The authors identify multi-event, evidential, and cross-document event factuality as future research directions.
